newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian provincial premiers to revive unity debate.
newsitem.headline: Canadian provincial premiers to revive unity debate.

text.p: The leaders of Canada's nine English-speaking provinces cautiously revived the long-running fight over national unity and French-speaking Quebec's ambitions to become independent.

The premiers agreed on Friday to hold informal talks on how they might address Quebec's concerns, but said the still unscheduled gathering will not include Lucien Bouchard, Quiebec's pro-separatist premier.

Bouchard immediately cast doubt that the session would produce any result that would make Quebec want to remain part of Canada or end the dispute that has clouded the country's politics and economy for years.

The nine premiers also cautioned against expecting too much from the meeting, adding that it was simply to hear ideas on how their provinces might address Quebec's fears that its society cannot survive within an English-dominated country.
"We're going to see what the state of play is and that's all we're going to be doing," said New Brunswick Premier Frank McKenna, whose bilingual province borders Quebec.

The provincial leaders made their announcement at a news conference at the end of a two-day annual meeting. Bouchard had threatened to walk out if national unity was discussed but he was on hand for the announcement.

Quebec's secessionists were defeated by a razor thin margin in a sovereignty referendum in October 1995. It was the second time in 15 years that the separatists had been rebuffed in a referendum but they have continued to gain strength.
Quebec is expected to hold a provincial election sometime in 1998 -- a probable precursor to another referendum on whether it should break away from the rest of Canada.
Bouchard dismissed past attempts to piece together Canada's fragile constitutional puzzle as futile efforts that had weakened Quebec's position within the Canadian federation.

"When you think about the repatriation of the constitution in 1982, Meech Lake and Charlottetown, you saw the premiers of Quebec, Mr. (Rene) Levesque and Mr. (Robert) Bourassa who were badly burned," he declared.
"Quebec got out of it weaker, and I will not add to the weakness of Quebec," Bouchard said, explaining why he had declined an invitation to attend the planned unity meeting.

"With all due respect to those who are undertaking this exercise, I think to hold new consultation will lead to no more than repetitions of everything we have heard over and over ad nauseum," Bouchard said.

Saskatchewan Premier Roy Romanow, a veteran of the national unity debate, said the planned meeting was a first step in mobilizing Canada's dispirited federalist forces -- especially those within Quebec.

"I'm happy about this decision by the premiers because we will end what I have feared is a sleepwalk into the inevitability of the next Quebec election and what might flow from the next Quebec election," Romanow said.

The premiers said federal officials were not invited to the meeting, but they downplayed the significance of that decision. Prime Minister Jean Chretien has been sharply attacked for is handling of the last Quebec referendum.

Opposition has been growing in western Canada to the federal government's efforts to address Quebec's concerns, and at least one western premier indicated he was doubtful a new solution to the unity question could be found.
"I haven't seen anything that will solve the problem," said Gary Filmon, of Manitoba.

The nine premiers tried to stress during the annual meeting that they were already taking steps to keep Quebec happy, approving a proposal to shift managerial control for several key social programs from Ottawa to the provinces.
Bouchard rejected that proposal, saying it gave the federal government too much control over Quebec's affairs. "Quebec cannot accept this," he told reporters.
